    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Runtime operator handoff and shared observability contract\",\n  \"space\": \"eng-serving-runtime\",\n  \"author\": \"Priya Ramanathan\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2024-11-12\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-01-15\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Ethan Park\",\n    \"Marina Kovalev\",\n    \"Jonas Becker\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"operator-handoff\",\n    \"observability\",\n    \"runbook\",\n    \"slo\",\n    \"profiling\",\n    \"benchmarks\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026\",\n    \"/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025\",\n    \"/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026\"\n  ],\n  \"content\": \"Overview\\n\\nPurpose: This page defines the operator handoff checklist and the shared observability contract used by runtime engineers, SREs, and oncall to run, tune and troubleshoot Redwood's serving runtime. The contract covers the set of metrics, traces, profiling artifacts, benchmark markers, release-note signals, and known-issue flags that must be produced and consumed during a feature rollout or operational incident.\\n\\nScope\\n- Applies to runtime components that live in the serving process: dispatcher, kernel dispatcher, KV cache, scheduler, admission controller, telemetry adapter.\\n- Intended consumers: oncall SRE, runtime owners, release engineers, customer-facing support.\\n\\nHigh-level principles\\n1) Contract-first telemetry: every feature must document the telem signals it produces and the expected shapes before canary.\\n2) Lightweight by default: default collection is cheap; heavy profiling is opt-in and gated by the profiling playbook.\\n3) Deterministic handoff: deployments must meet the handoff checklist before they are considered live for SRE ownership.\\n\\nOperator handoff checklist (must be completed by owning team before SRE takeover)\\n1. Architecture summary and README: service-level diagram, primary components, and request path.\\n2. SLOs and budgets: Token-level P50/P95/P99, request success rate, and error budget allocation. See SLO table below.\\n3. Runbook links: runbooks for slow kernels, memory pressure, eviction, and graceful shutdown (links).\\n4. Baseline benchmarks: representative benchmark IDs and artifact links produced by the benchmark suite.\\n5. Observability contract: list of metrics/traces/logs produced and required alerts.\\n6. Profiling recipe: sample profiling command and storage location for artifacts.\\n7. Feature flags and gating matrix: flags to revert/disable and required rollout steps.\\n8. Known issues: documented regressions and mitigations.\\n9. Oncall contact and escalation path.\\n\\nSLO summary (example table)\\n| Metric | Target | Measurement window | Owner |\\n| Token latency P95 (generation) | <= 140ms | 1h | runtime-kernel |\\n| Request end-to-end P99 | <= 350ms | 1h | runtime-dispatch |\\n| Request success rate | >= 99.92% | 24h | runtime-sre |\\n| Kernel error rate (per kernel) | <= 0.05% | 1h | runtime-kernel |\\n\\nRequired observability signals\\n- Metrics (timeseries):\\n  - runtime.requests.total, runtime.requests.latency_ms{p50,p95,p99}, runtime.kvcache.hits, runtime.kvcache.miss_rate, runtime.kernel.queue_length, runtime.kernel.active_kernels, runtime.kernel.evictions, runtime.dispatch.admission_rejections.\\n- Traces: distributed trace with root span = request.dispatch, child spans: route.resolve, kernel.execute[slice], kvcache.lookup, response.serialize. Each kernel.execute span must annotate kernel_id, input_seq_len, output_tokens, and kernel_hint_version.\\n- Logs: structured JSON logs with fields {request_id, trace_id, kernel_id, error_code, node_id, cohort}.\\n- Profiling artifacts: flamegraphs, nvprof summaries, kernel latency histograms, and memory-snapshot tarballs. Must include commit hash and benchmark id in filenames.\\n\\nProfiling playbook (quick recipe)\\n1. When: trigger profiling when P95 exceeds baseline by > 25% for 3 consecutive 5-minute buckets, or when kernel error rate spikes.\\n2. Sampling mode: start with lightweight sampling (1% of requests) using adaptive tracer.\\n3. Escalation: if signal persists, run an isolated micro-benchmark using the benchmark ID from the baseline (see example command).\\n4. Artifact retention: upload artifacts and add link to incident. Retain for 90 days by default.\\n\\nCommand examples\\n- Lightweight trace sampler (k8s job):\\n  kubectl -n runtime exec -it profiler -- /bin/sh -c \\\"profiler collect --sample-rate=0.01 --duration=15m --out=/tmp/prof-$COMMIT-$ID.tgz\\\"\\n\\n- Micro-benchmark run (local dev):\\n  ./benchctl run --suite=echo-mixed --concurrency=16 --seq-dist=\\\"(8:0.6,64:0.3,512:0.1)\\\" --commit=$COMMIT --artifact=bench-$COMMIT-$(date +%s).tgz\\n\\nBenchmark suite manifest (required fields for baseline artifact)\\n- bench_id: short identifier of benchmark (e.g., echo-mixed-20241112)\\n- commit_hash: runtime sha\\n- hardware_profile: e.g., a100s-40g, h100-80g.pci, t4-dense\\n- seq_distribution: brief summary\\n- batch_config: {batch_size, max_latency_ms} (recorded as YAML in artifact metadata)\\n\\nExample artifact metadata (YAML snippet)\\ncommit_hash: \\\"a1b2c3d4\\\"\\nhardware_profile: \\\"h100-80g.pci\\\"\\nbench_id: \\\"echo-mixed-20241112\\\"\\nseq_distribution: \\\"8:60%,64:30%,512:10%\\\"\\nbatch_config:\\\\n  batch_size: 8\\\\n  max_latency_ms: 120\\n\\nKernel scheduling tracing contract\\n- Kernel spans must include: kernel_id (stable id), kernel_version, kernel_hint, requested_seq_len, observed_concurrency, dispatch_slot_id.\\n- Scheduling decisions (admit/reject/hedge) must emit an event to the scheduling bus and write a trace annotation with decision_reason.\\n- Scheduler-level metrics to emit: kernel.wait_time_ms, kernel.exec_time_ms, kernel.preemptions, kernel.hedges_initiated.\\n\\nRelease note and canary signals\\n- Every runtime release must include a release note that lists: changed kernels, new scheduler heuristics, observability deltas (new metrics/traces), and benchmark regressions measured against the acceptance suite.\\n- Canary acceptance criteria (example): no P99 latency regression > 10% vs baseline, error rate <= baseline + 0.02%, no new disk or memory OOMs observed during canary window.\\n\\nKnown issues reporting format\\n- Include short description, impacted components, reproducibility steps, temporary mitigation, owner, and ETA for permanent fix. Example: \\n  - ID: KVC-2026-07\\n  - Summary: infrequent KV cache shard imbalance under multi-tenant spikes\\n  - Impact: increased cold misses and P95 latency blips\\n  - Mitigation: scale KVC shards or enable per-tenant eviction policy.\\n  - Owner: runtime-kv-team\\n  - ETA: 2026-02-28\\n\\nOperational runbooks and playbook links (must be present)\\n1. slow-kernel-detection-and-hotfix-playbook (link)\\n2. memory-pressure-incident-triage-and-recovery-playbook (link)\\n3. runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook (link)\\n4. quantitative-burst-slo-simulation-and-cost-sampling (benchmarks)\\n5. graceful-shutdown-and-session-drain-runbook (link)\\n\\nOwner & escalation matrix\\n- Primary owner: runtime-platform (pager: oncall-runtime-platform)\\n- Secondary (kernel): runtime-kernel (pager: oncall-runtime-kernel)\\n- SRE escalation: follow standard oncall escalation (1st hour - page primary, 1-3 hours - page secondary, >3 hours - page eng manager).\\n\\nChecklist for post-incident follow-up (postmortem inputs)\\n1. Collect baseline benchmarks (pre/post) and profiler artifacts.\\n2. Annotate traces with incident timeline and decision points.\\n3. Run regression bench suite to validate fix.\\n4. Update runbooks and observability contract if gaps discovered.\\n\\nAppendix: quick reference (search tokens)\\n- Search metric prefixes: runtime.*, kernel.*, kvcache.*\\n- Benchmark artifact prefix: bench-\\n- Profile artifact prefix: prof-\\n- Incident label: runtime-incident-YYYYMMDD\\n\\nRelated docs and references\\n- Profiling playbook (recommended sequence): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025\\n- Benchmark acceptance suite: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026\\n- Scheduler design notes: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026\\n\\nEnd of document\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_be35ae65a0ee488f9e547f1a07cc4f11\"\n}",

{
  "title": "Runtime operator handoff and shared observability contract",
  "space": "eng-serving-runtime",
  "author": "Priya Ramanathan",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2024-11-12",
  "last_updated": "2026-01-15",
  "reviewers": [
    "Ethan Park",
    "Marina Kovalev",
    "Jonas Becker"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "operator-handoff",
    "observability",
    "runbook",
    "slo",
    "profiling",
    "benchmarks"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "related_pages": [
    "/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026",
    "/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025",
    "/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026"
  ],
  "content": "Overview

Purpose: This page defines the operator handoff checklist and the shared observability contract used by runtime engineers, SREs, and oncall to run, tune and troubleshoot Redwood's serving runtime. The contract covers the set of metrics, traces, profiling artifacts, benchmark markers, release-note signals, and known-issue flags that must be produced and consumed during a feature rollout or operational incident.

Scope
- Applies to runtime components that live in the serving process: dispatcher, kernel dispatcher, KV cache, scheduler, admission controller, telemetry adapter.
- Intended consumers: oncall SRE, runtime owners, release engineers, customer-facing support.

High-level principles
1) Contract-first telemetry: every feature must document the telem signals it produces and the expected shapes before canary.
2) Lightweight by default: default collection is cheap; heavy profiling is opt-in and gated by the profiling playbook.
3) Deterministic handoff: deployments must meet the handoff checklist before they are considered live for SRE ownership.

Operator handoff checklist (must be completed by owning team before SRE takeover)
1. Architecture summary and README: service-level diagram, primary components, and request path.
2. SLOs and budgets: Token-level P50/P95/P99, request success rate, and error budget allocation. See SLO table below.
3. Runbook links: runbooks for slow kernels, memory pressure, eviction, and graceful shutdown (links).
4. Baseline benchmarks: representative benchmark IDs and artifact links produced by the benchmark suite.
5. Observability contract: list of metrics/traces/logs produced and required alerts.
6. Profiling recipe: sample profiling command and storage location for artifacts.
7. Feature flags and gating matrix: flags to revert/disable and required rollout steps.
8. Known issues: documented regressions and mitigations.
9. Oncall contact and escalation path.

SLO summary (example table)
| Metric | Target | Measurement window | Owner |
| Token latency P95 (generation) | <= 140ms | 1h | runtime-kernel |
| Request end-to-end P99 | <= 350ms | 1h | runtime-dispatch |
| Request success rate | >= 99.92% | 24h | runtime-sre |
| Kernel error rate (per kernel) | <= 0.05% | 1h | runtime-kernel |

Required observability signals
- Metrics (timeseries):
  - runtime.requests.total, runtime.requests.latency_ms{p50,p95,p99}, runtime.kvcache.hits, runtime.kvcache.miss_rate, runtime.kernel.queue_length, runtime.kernel.active_kernels, runtime.kernel.evictions, runtime.dispatch.admission_rejections.
- Traces: distributed trace with root span = request.dispatch, child spans: route.resolve, kernel.execute[slice], kvcache.lookup, response.serialize. Each kernel.execute span must annotate kernel_id, input_seq_len, output_tokens, and kernel_hint_version.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with fields {request_id, trace_id, kernel_id, error_code, node_id, cohort}.
- Profiling artifacts: flamegraphs, nvprof summaries, kernel latency histograms, and memory-snapshot tarballs. Must include commit hash and benchmark id in filenames.

Profiling playbook (quick recipe)
1. When: trigger profiling when P95 exceeds baseline by > 25% for 3 consecutive 5-minute buckets, or when kernel error rate spikes.
2. Sampling mode: start with lightweight sampling (1% of requests) using adaptive tracer.
3. Escalation: if signal persists, run an isolated micro-benchmark using the benchmark ID from the baseline (see example command).
4. Artifact retention: upload artifacts and add link to incident. Retain for 90 days by default.

Command examples
- Lightweight trace sampler (k8s job):
  kubectl -n runtime exec -it profiler -- /bin/sh -c "profiler collect --sample-rate=0.01 --duration=15m --out=/tmp/prof-$COMMIT-$ID.tgz"

- Micro-benchmark run (local dev):
  ./benchctl run --suite=echo-mixed --concurrency=16 --seq-dist="(8:0.6,64:0.3,512:0.1)" --commit=$COMMIT --artifact=bench-$COMMIT-$(date +%s).tgz

Benchmark suite manifest (required fields for baseline artifact)
- bench_id: short identifier of benchmark (e.g., echo-mixed-20241112)
- commit_hash: runtime sha
- hardware_profile: e.g., a100s-40g, h100-80g.pci, t4-dense
- seq_distribution: brief summary
- batch_config: {batch_size, max_latency_ms} (recorded as YAML in artifact metadata)

Example artifact metadata (YAML snippet)
commit_hash: "a1b2c3d4"
hardware_profile: "h100-80g.pci"
bench_id: "echo-mixed-20241112"
seq_distribution: "8:60%,64:30%,512:10%"
batch_config:\n  batch_size: 8\n  max_latency_ms: 120

Kernel scheduling tracing contract
- Kernel spans must include: kernel_id (stable id), kernel_version, kernel_hint, requested_seq_len, observed_concurrency, dispatch_slot_id.
- Scheduling decisions (admit/reject/hedge) must emit an event to the scheduling bus and write a trace annotation with decision_reason.
- Scheduler-level metrics to emit: kernel.wait_time_ms, kernel.exec_time_ms, kernel.preemptions, kernel.hedges_initiated.

Release note and canary signals
- Every runtime release must include a release note that lists: changed kernels, new scheduler heuristics, observability deltas (new metrics/traces), and benchmark regressions measured against the acceptance suite.
- Canary acceptance criteria (example): no P99 latency regression > 10% vs baseline, error rate <= baseline + 0.02%, no new disk or memory OOMs observed during canary window.

Known issues reporting format
- Include short description, impacted components, reproducibility steps, temporary mitigation, owner, and ETA for permanent fix. Example: 
  - ID: KVC-2026-07
  - Summary: infrequent KV cache shard imbalance under multi-tenant spikes
  - Impact: increased cold misses and P95 latency blips
  - Mitigation: scale KVC shards or enable per-tenant eviction policy.
  - Owner: runtime-kv-team
  - ETA: 2026-02-28

Operational runbooks and playbook links (must be present)
1. slow-kernel-detection-and-hotfix-playbook (link)
2. memory-pressure-incident-triage-and-recovery-playbook (link)
3. runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook (link)
4. quantitative-burst-slo-simulation-and-cost-sampling (benchmarks)
5. graceful-shutdown-and-session-drain-runbook (link)

Owner & escalation matrix
- Primary owner: runtime-platform (pager: oncall-runtime-platform)
- Secondary (kernel): runtime-kernel (pager: oncall-runtime-kernel)
- SRE escalation: follow standard oncall escalation (1st hour - page primary, 1-3 hours - page secondary, >3 hours - page eng manager).

Checklist for post-incident follow-up (postmortem inputs)
1. Collect baseline benchmarks (pre/post) and profiler artifacts.
2. Annotate traces with incident timeline and decision points.
3. Run regression bench suite to validate fix.
4. Update runbooks and observability contract if gaps discovered.

Appendix: quick reference (search tokens)
- Search metric prefixes: runtime.*, kernel.*, kvcache.*
- Benchmark artifact prefix: bench-
- Profile artifact prefix: prof-
- Incident label: runtime-incident-YYYYMMDD

Related docs and references
- Profiling playbook (recommended sequence): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025
- Benchmark acceptance suite: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026
- Scheduler design notes: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026

End of document

    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Operational Resilience: Scenario Library, Runbooks, and Customer Communication Kits\",\n  \"space\": \"oncall-and-incident-response\",\n  \"author\": \"Aisha Patel\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2024-11-15\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-02-20\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Diego Martinez\",\n    \"Chen Li\",\n    \"Sofia Nguyen\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"runbook\",\n    \"game-day\",\n    \"incident-process\",\n    \"communications\",\n    \"SLOs\"\n  ],\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"/confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets-2025\",\n    \"/confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-comm-and-postmortem-framework-2026\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"body\": \"Summary\\nThis page is a consolidated, actionable reference for operational resilience: a scenario library (high-level triage + dedicated runbooks), game-day / exercise plans, on-call rotation guidance, and ready-made customer and status-page communication kits. It is intended for first responders, on-call SREs, incident commanders, product on-call engineers, and customer success teams.\\n\\nGoals\\n- Reduce time-to-diagnosis for common classes of incidents (latency spikes, model degradation, capacity exhaustion, auth/ingress failures).\\n- Standardize communications to customers and internal stakeholders.\\n- Provide measurable exercise templates for improving SLO attainment and runbook coverage.\\n\\nHow to use this page\\n1) Read the severity matrix below to classify incidents.\\n2) Follow the scenario checklist for the matching incident class.\\n3) Escalate to the runbook owner and apply runbook steps.\\n4) Use the communication templates verbatim (edit only the bracketed fields).\\n5) After resolution, run the postmortem checklist and schedule a blameless review within 72 hours.\\n\\nIncident severity matrix (quick reference)\\n- SEV-0 (Platform outage): Service unavailable across multiple regions or core API returns >50% 5xx across customers for >5 minutes.\\n- SEV-1 (Major degradation): Latency >2x P99 target or error rate >5% for production endpoints impacting multiple customers for >15 minutes.\\n- SEV-2 (Partial impact): Single-customer outage, queued requests, or feature regressions reducing throughput or model quality for a subset of traffic.\\n- SEV-3 (Minor): Nonblocking bugs, dashboard/metrics gaps, or cosmetic UI issues.\\n\\nSLOs and alerting thresholds (examples we enforce)\\n| SLO | Goal | Alert threshold | Pager escalation |\\n|-----|------|----------------|-----------------|\\n| API availability (global) | 99.95% monthly | Incident if 5xx rate >20% for 5 minutes | SEV-0 |\\n| P99 latency (text-generation) | <1200ms | Alert if P99 >2500ms for 10 minutes | SEV-1 |\\n| Embedding throughput (dedicated pool) | 95% of committed capacity | Alert if queued >30% for 15 min | SEV-1 |\\n\\nScenario library (selection of high-value scenarios)\\n1) Large-scale latency spike (multi-region)\\n- Typical cause: kernel regression, autoscaler misconfiguration, cold caches, network flapping.\\n- Initial triage checklist:\\n  1. Confirm alert: check /metrics/api/5xx_rate and /metrics/latency/p99 across regions.\\n  2. Identify scope: run `curl -sS https://ops-api.internal/telemetry?range=15m` or open Grafana dashboard \\\"API-Latency-Overview\\\".\\n  3. Check recent deploys: `git log -n 5 --pretty=format:\\\"%h %s\\\" --deploy-tag` and the rollout dashboard.\\n  4. Verify cache hit rates: /metrics/cache/prefix_hit_rate.\\n  5. If CPU/GPU throttling present, check node metrics: `kubectl top pods -n runtime` and `nvidia-smi` on affected hosts.\\n- Primary runbook: eng-serving-runtime/diagnose-latency-spike (owner: runtime oncall).\\n- Quick mitigations (apply while diagnosing):\\n  - Temporarily reduce batch size to limit tail latency: `PATCH /internal/configuration` body `{\\\\\\\"batch_size\\\\\\\": 1}` (apply to affected model pool).\\n  - Increase autoscaler target min replicas for the pool: `infractl autoscale set --pool <pool-id> --min 4`.\\n  - Failover traffic to standby region following the smart routing playbook (see below).\\n\\n2) Capacity exhaustion on Dedicated pools\\n- Typical cause: unexpected customer load, quota misreporting, autoscaler failure.\\n- Initial triage checklist:\\n  1. Check pool utilization: Grafana \\\"Dedicated-Pool-Utilization\\\" and `infractl pool describe <pool-id>`.\\n  2. Confirm quota accounting: `billing-api /pools/<id>/usage`.\\n  3. Identify heavy tenants with `kafka audit` and `tenant-usage-service` query.\\n- Primary runbook: eng-sre/dedicated-pool-backpressure-and-eviction (owner: infra).\\n- Quick mitigations:\\n  - Enable backpressure for non-critical routes: `policyctl set backpressure --routes pattern=embeddings:* --level moderate`.\\n  - Activate defined bursts if available: `infractl bursts enable --pool <pool-id> --duration 10m`.\\n  - Notify on-call CS rep to check if affected customer has emergency burst credit.\\n\\n3) Authentication / onboarding ingress failures\\n- Typical cause: KMS outage, mis-rotated keys, proxy misconfig.\\n- Triage checklist:\\n  1. Verify KMS status and keyring: `aws kms get-key-rotation-status --key-id <key>` or HSM dashboard.\\n  2. Check gateway logs: `kubectl logs gateway-0 -n ingress | grep AuthService`.\\n  3. Validate token issuance: `authz-cli validate --token <sample-token>`.\\n- Primary runbook: security-and-compliance/authz-failure-playbook (owner: security).\\n\\nRunbook structure (standardized)\\n- Title (clear): short phrase + owner team\\n- Symptoms: bullet list\\n- Impact: how to determine scope / SLO hit\\n- Preconditions: required ACLs, diagnostic tools, runbook prerequisites\\n- Step-by-step remediation (numbered) with commands and rollback guidance\\n- Post-resolution actions: tickets, customer notifications, follow-up tasks\\n- When to escalate: explicit signals (e.g., >10% traffic loss after 15m)\\n\\nRunbook example excerpt: diagnose-service-degradation (short form)\\n1) Confirm the incident and set a bridge: `incidentctl create --severity SEV-1 --summary \\\\\\\"P99 >2500ms for text-generation\\\\\\\"`\\n2) Assign roles: Incident Commander (IC), Lead Triage Engineer, Communication Lead, Exec Liaison.\\n3) Collect evidence: attach trace IDs, request samples, and Grafana links to the incident.\\n4) Attempt a safe rollback of the last model-serving release: `deployctl rollback --service runtime --to-tag <previous>` (ensure canary traffic is healthy first).\\n5) If rollback not possible, apply throttling policy: `policyctl throttle --route /v1/generate --percent 50`.\\n6) Monitor the effect for 5 minutes; document metrics snapshot.\\n\\nCommunication kits (templates)\\n- Internal Slack (immediate):\\n  > [INCIDENT] SEV-1: P99 latency for text-generation >2500ms across us-west/us-east. IC: @aisha, Bridge: <bridge-link>. Actions: rollback underway.\\n\\n- Status page public template (initial):\\n  Title: Service Degradation: Text Generation Latency\\n  Impact: Users may experience higher-than-normal response times for text generation.\\n  Affected products: Redwood API (text generation)\\n  Start time: [YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC]\\n  Current status: Investigating\\n  Next update: in 15 minutes\\n  Root cause: TBD\\n\\n- Customer-facing email (short update):\\n  Subject: Update: Redwood API - degraded text-generation performance\\n\\n  Hi [Customer Name],\\n\\n  We are investigating a performance degradation affecting text-generation requests. Our SRE team has identified elevated P99 latency and is executing a rollback and failover plan. We will provide another update within 15 minutes.\\n\\n  Impact: increased response times; requests are not timing out.\\n  Actions in progress: rollback of last deploy, targeted traffic routing, and autoscaler adjustments.\\n\\n  Contact: [customer-success-email] or reply to this thread.\\n\\n  \\u2014 Redwood Inference Operations\\n\\nCustomer comms guidance\\n- Use plain language; avoid root-cause speculation until confirmed.\\n- Avoid technical dumps in the first 2 updates; provide timeline and mitigation steps instead.\\n- Escalate to the Customer Success lead for any enterprise customer with SLA exposure or regulatory constraints.\\n\\nPost-incident process (postmortem checklist)\\n1) Create a postmortem doc using the template (link: /confluence/templates/postmortem).\\n2) Fill in timeline (UTC) with evidence and decision points.\\n3) Tag code/infra changes with PRs and links.\\n4) Quantify customer impact: number of customers affected, error volume, SLO burn.\\n5) Define care-plan for any impacted enterprise customers (owner: CS).\\n6) Assign action items with owners and target dates; include verification criteria.\\n7) Present summary in weekly FRR (fault review) with the three most important takeaways.\\n\\nOn-call rotation & handoff standards\\n- Rotation length: 1 week for primary SREs; 2-week swing for platform leads.\\n- Coverage model: primary, secondary, and overflow (engineering floater).\\n- Handoff checklist (to be completed in Slack and incident ticket):\\n  - Current on-call status and pager routes active\\n  - Ongoing incidents with severity and short status\\n  - Scheduled maintenance and expected noise windows\\n  - Key contact details for escalation (CS lead, legal, security, executive liaison)\\n  - Link to runbook(s) used today and any temporary mitigations applied\\n\\nGame Day / Exercise curriculum (quarterly recommended)\\n- Frequency: quarterly mandatory game day for each SRE and runtime engineering pair.\\n- Example exercise: Region failover simulation\\n  - Goal: verify smart routing and stateful KV cache replay under failover.\\n  - Preconditions: synthetic traffic harness enabled, canary tokens, simulated region outage toggled via `infractl region-outage simulate --region us-west1`.\\n  - Steps: trigger outage, failover traffic, validate request success for 5k synthetic requests, observe cache warmup time, and measure P99.\\n  - Success criteria: failover completes without >2% additional error rate and less than 3x P99 latency for the first 5 minutes.\\n- After-action review: publish exercise notes, update related runbooks, and create Jira tickets for any gaps.\\n\\nStatus page update cadence and responsibilities\\n- When incident declared SEV-1+: update status page within 10 minutes (initial), then every 15 minutes until mitigation, then hourly during remediation, and final update with root cause and postmortem link.\\n- Owner: Communication Lead (role assigned in incident).\\n\\nEscalation matrix (condensed)\\n- SEV-0: IC -> CTO -> Legal & CS -> Exec on-call.\\n- SEV-1: IC -> Eng Manager (runtime/infra) -> CS lead.\\n- SEV-2: IC -> Team on-call -> Product PM.\\n- Escalation triggers: sustained SLO degradation >30 minutes, legal/regulatory exposure, or customer outage with SLA violation.\\n\\nOperational tooling & useful commands\\n- incidentctl: create/annotate incident tickets and bridges (`incidentctl create --severity SEV-1 --summary \\\\\\\"...\\\\\\\"`).\\n- infractl: pool and region controls (`infractl autoscale set`, `infractl pool describe`).\\n- policyctl: runtime routing and throttling policies.\\n- deployctl: safe rollbacks and canary controls.\\n- Example: failover to standby region\\n  1) `policyctl route set --svc api --to-region us-east1 --weight 100`\\n  2) Monitor `curl -sS https://ops-api.internal/telemetry?range=5m`\\n  3) If errors increase, revert `policyctl route set --svc api --to-region us-west1 --weight 100`\\n\\nRunbook maintenance cadence\\n- Owners must review runbooks they own every 6 months or after a game-day if exercise exposed gaps.\\n- Retire or rewrite runbooks with >3 stakeholder-reported failures in a quarter.\\n\\nAppendix: incident communication templates (copy-and-paste)\\n- Initial internal incident creation (IC uses this in bridge):\\n  > Title: [SEV-1] <short summary>\\n  > Bridge: <bridge-link>\\n  > IC: @<name>\\n  > Roles: Triage, CommLead, ExecLiaison\\n  > Evidence: Grafana links, sample trace IDs\\n\\n- Final postmortem summary (public-friendly)\\n  Title: Postmortem: [SEV-1] Text-generation latency spike \\u2014 [YYYY-MM-DD]\\n  Summary: Short non-technical summary of what happened, impact, and customer-facing remediation.\\n  Impact: Affected 12 customers, increase in P99 to 3.2s for 7 minutes; no data loss.\\n  Root cause: A scheduling regression in kernel selector after traffic shift caused increased tail latency.\\n  Remediation: Reverted the faulty selection algorithm; added additional unit + integration tests; deployment gating adjusted.\\n  Action items: list with owners and due dates.\\n\\nContacts and ownership (quick directory)\\n- Incident Commander rotation: sashas@redwood.ai (primary), aisha@redwood.ai (backup)\\n- Runtime oncall: #runtime-oncall (Slack)\\n- Infra oncall: infra-oncall@redwood.ai\\n- CS escalation: cs-leads@redwood.ai\\n\\nDocument history and governance\\nThis page replaces ad-hoc checklists and consolidates communication kits and scenario templates. Owners must keep the page up-to-date and include any new templates derived from customer-facing incidents.\\n\\nIf you find missing scenarios or need an additional runbook added to the library, open a PR on the docs repo and ping @aisha for review.\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_57f9b542665c4c82b8b2648da13dfb0e\"\n}",

document.title: Operational Resilience: Scenario Library, Runbooks, and Customer Communication Kits
document.content:
{
  "title": "Operational Resilience: Scenario Library, Runbooks, and Customer Communication Kits",
  "space": "oncall-and-incident-response",
  "author": "Aisha Patel",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2024-11-15",
  "last_updated": "2026-02-20",
  "reviewers": [
    "Diego Martinez",
    "Chen Li",
    "Sofia Nguyen"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "runbook",
    "game-day",
    "incident-process",
    "communications",
    "SLOs"
  ],
  "related_pages": [
    "/confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets-2025",
    "/confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-comm-and-postmortem-framework-2026"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "body": "Summary
This page is a consolidated, actionable reference for operational resilience: a scenario library (high-level triage + dedicated runbooks), game-day / exercise plans, on-call rotation guidance, and ready-made customer and status-page communication kits. It is intended for first responders, on-call SREs, incident commanders, product on-call engineers, and customer success teams.

Goals
- Reduce time-to-diagnosis for common classes of incidents (latency spikes, model degradation, capacity exhaustion, auth/ingress failures).
- Standardize communications to customers and internal stakeholders.
- Provide measurable exercise templates for improving SLO attainment and runbook coverage.

How to use this page
1) Read the severity matrix below to classify incidents.
2) Follow the scenario checklist for the matching incident class.
3) Escalate to the runbook owner and apply runbook steps.
4) Use the communication templates verbatim (edit only the bracketed fields).
5) After resolution, run the postmortem checklist and schedule a blameless review within 72 hours.

Incident severity matrix (quick reference)
- SEV-0 (Platform outage): Service unavailable across multiple regions or core API returns >50% 5xx across customers for >5 minutes.
- SEV-1 (Major degradation): Latency >2x P99 target or error rate >5% for production endpoints impacting multiple customers for >15 minutes.
- SEV-2 (Partial impact): Single-customer outage, queued requests, or feature regressions reducing throughput or model quality for a subset of traffic.
- SEV-3 (Minor): Nonblocking bugs, dashboard/metrics gaps, or cosmetic UI issues.

SLOs and alerting thresholds (examples we enforce)
| SLO | Goal | Alert threshold | Pager escalation |
|-----|------|----------------|-----------------|
| API availability (global) | 99.95% monthly | Incident if 5xx rate >20% for 5 minutes | SEV-0 |
| P99 latency (text-generation) | <1200ms | Alert if P99 >2500ms for 10 minutes | SEV-1 |
| Embedding throughput (dedicated pool) | 95% of committed capacity | Alert if queued >30% for 15 min | SEV-1 |

Scenario library (selection of high-value scenarios)
1) Large-scale latency spike (multi-region)
- Typical cause: kernel regression, autoscaler misconfiguration, cold caches, network flapping.
- Initial triage checklist:
  1. Confirm alert: check /metrics/api/5xx_rate and /metrics/latency/p99 across regions.
  2. Identify scope: run `curl -sS https://ops-api.internal/telemetry?range=15m` or open Grafana dashboard "API-Latency-Overview".
  3. Check recent deploys: `git log -n 5 --pretty=format:"%h %s" --deploy-tag` and the rollout dashboard.
  4. Verify cache hit rates: /metrics/cache/prefix_hit_rate.
  5. If CPU/GPU throttling present, check node metrics: `kubectl top pods -n runtime` and `nvidia-smi` on affected hosts.
- Primary runbook: eng-serving-runtime/diagnose-latency-spike (owner: runtime oncall).
- Quick mitigations (apply while diagnosing):
  - Temporarily reduce batch size to limit tail latency: `PATCH /internal/configuration` body `{\"batch_size\": 1}` (apply to affected model pool).
  - Increase autoscaler target min replicas for the pool: `infractl autoscale set --pool <pool-id> --min 4`.
  - Failover traffic to standby region following the smart routing playbook (see below).

2) Capacity exhaustion on Dedicated pools
- Typical cause: unexpected customer load, quota misreporting, autoscaler failure.
- Initial triage checklist:
  1. Check pool utilization: Grafana "Dedicated-Pool-Utilization" and `infractl pool describe <pool-id>`.
  2. Confirm quota accounting: `billing-api /pools/<id>/usage`.
  3. Identify heavy tenants with `kafka audit` and `tenant-usage-service` query.
- Primary runbook: eng-sre/dedicated-pool-backpressure-and-eviction (owner: infra).
- Quick mitigations:
  - Enable backpressure for non-critical routes: `policyctl set backpressure --routes pattern=embeddings:* --level moderate`.
  - Activate defined bursts if available: `infractl bursts enable --pool <pool-id> --duration 10m`.
  - Notify on-call CS rep to check if affected customer has emergency burst credit.

3) Authentication / onboarding ingress failures
- Typical cause: KMS outage, mis-rotated keys, proxy misconfig.
- Triage checklist:
  1. Verify KMS status and keyring: `aws kms get-key-rotation-status --key-id <key>` or HSM dashboard.
  2. Check gateway logs: `kubectl logs gateway-0 -n ingress | grep AuthService`.
  3. Validate token issuance: `authz-cli validate --token <sample-token>`.
- Primary runbook: security-and-compliance/authz-failure-playbook (owner: security).

Runbook structure (standardized)
- Title (clear): short phrase + owner team
- Symptoms: bullet list
- Impact: how to determine scope / SLO hit
- Preconditions: required ACLs, diagnostic tools, runbook prerequisites
- Step-by-step remediation (numbered) with commands and rollback guidance
- Post-resolution actions: tickets, customer notifications, follow-up tasks
- When to escalate: explicit signals (e.g., >10% traffic loss after 15m)

Runbook example excerpt: diagnose-service-degradation (short form)
1) Confirm the incident and set a bridge: `incidentctl create --severity SEV-1 --summary \"P99 >2500ms for text-generation\"`
2) Assign roles: Incident Commander (IC), Lead Triage Engineer, Communication Lead, Exec Liaison.
3) Collect evidence: attach trace IDs, request samples, and Grafana links to the incident.
4) Attempt a safe rollback of the last model-serving release: `deployctl rollback --service runtime --to-tag <previous>` (ensure canary traffic is healthy first).
5) If rollback not possible, apply throttling policy: `policyctl throttle --route /v1/generate --percent 50`.
6) Monitor the effect for 5 minutes; document metrics snapshot.

Communication kits (templates)
- Internal Slack (immediate):
  > [INCIDENT] SEV-1: P99 latency for text-generation >2500ms across us-west/us-east. IC: @aisha, Bridge: <bridge-link>. Actions: rollback underway.

- Status page public template (initial):
  Title: Service Degradation: Text Generation Latency
  Impact: Users may experience higher-than-normal response times for text generation.
  Affected products: Redwood API (text generation)
  Start time: [YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC]
  Current status: Investigating
  Next update: in 15 minutes
  Root cause: TBD

- Customer-facing email (short update):
  Subject: Update: Redwood API - degraded text-generation performance

  Hi [Customer Name],

  We are investigating a performance degradation affecting text-generation requests. Our SRE team has identified elevated P99 latency and is executing a rollback and failover plan. We will provide another update within 15 minutes.

  Impact: increased response times; requests are not timing out.
  Actions in progress: rollback of last deploy, targeted traffic routing, and autoscaler adjustments.

  Contact: [customer-success-email] or reply to this thread.

  — Redwood Inference Operations

Customer comms guidance
- Use plain language; avoid root-cause speculation until confirmed.
- Avoid technical dumps in the first 2 updates; provide timeline and mitigation steps instead.
- Escalate to the Customer Success lead for any enterprise customer with SLA exposure or regulatory constraints.

Post-incident process (postmortem checklist)
1) Create a postmortem doc using the template (link: /confluence/templates/postmortem).
2) Fill in timeline (UTC) with evidence and decision points.
3) Tag code/infra changes with PRs and links.
4) Quantify customer impact: number of customers affected, error volume, SLO burn.
5) Define care-plan for any impacted enterprise customers (owner: CS).
6) Assign action items with owners and target dates; include verification criteria.
7) Present summary in weekly FRR (fault review) with the three most important takeaways.

On-call rotation & handoff standards
- Rotation length: 1 week for primary SREs; 2-week swing for platform leads.
- Coverage model: primary, secondary, and overflow (engineering floater).
- Handoff checklist (to be completed in Slack and incident ticket):
  - Current on-call status and pager routes active
  - Ongoing incidents with severity and short status
  - Scheduled maintenance and expected noise windows
  - Key contact details for escalation (CS lead, legal, security, executive liaison)
  - Link to runbook(s) used today and any temporary mitigations applied

Game Day / Exercise curriculum (quarterly recommended)
- Frequency: quarterly mandatory game day for each SRE and runtime engineering pair.
- Example exercise: Region failover simulation
  - Goal: verify smart routing and stateful KV cache replay under failover.
  - Preconditions: synthetic traffic harness enabled, canary tokens, simulated region outage toggled via `infractl region-outage simulate --region us-west1`.
  - Steps: trigger outage, failover traffic, validate request success for 5k synthetic requests, observe cache warmup time, and measure P99.
  - Success criteria: failover completes without >2% additional error rate and less than 3x P99 latency for the first 5 minutes.
- After-action review: publish exercise notes, update related runbooks, and create Jira tickets for any gaps.

Status page update cadence and responsibilities
- When incident declared SEV-1+: update status page within 10 minutes (initial), then every 15 minutes until mitigation, then hourly during remediation, and final update with root cause and postmortem link.
- Owner: Communication Lead (role assigned in incident).

Escalation matrix (condensed)
- SEV-0: IC -> CTO -> Legal & CS -> Exec on-call.
- SEV-1: IC -> Eng Manager (runtime/infra) -> CS lead.
- SEV-2: IC -> Team on-call -> Product PM.
- Escalation triggers: sustained SLO degradation >30 minutes, legal/regulatory exposure, or customer outage with SLA violation.

Operational tooling & useful commands
- incidentctl: create/annotate incident tickets and bridges (`incidentctl create --severity SEV-1 --summary \"...\"`).
- infractl: pool and region controls (`infractl autoscale set`, `infractl pool describe`).
- policyctl: runtime routing and throttling policies.
- deployctl: safe rollbacks and canary controls.
- Example: failover to standby region
  1) `policyctl route set --svc api --to-region us-east1 --weight 100`
  2) Monitor `curl -sS https://ops-api.internal/telemetry?range=5m`
  3) If errors increase, revert `policyctl route set --svc api --to-region us-west1 --weight 100`

Runbook maintenance cadence
- Owners must review runbooks they own every 6 months or after a game-day if exercise exposed gaps.
- Retire or rewrite runbooks with >3 stakeholder-reported failures in a quarter.

Appendix: incident communication templates (copy-and-paste)
- Initial internal incident creation (IC uses this in bridge):
  > Title: [SEV-1] <short summary>
  > Bridge: <bridge-link>
  > IC: @<name>
  > Roles: Triage, CommLead, ExecLiaison
  > Evidence: Grafana links, sample trace IDs

- Final postmortem summary (public-friendly)
  Title: Postmortem: [SEV-1] Text-generation latency spike — [YYYY-MM-DD]
  Summary: Short non-technical summary of what happened, impact, and customer-facing remediation.
  Impact: Affected 12 customers, increase in P99 to 3.2s for 7 minutes; no data loss.
  Root cause: A scheduling regression in kernel selector after traffic shift caused increased tail latency.
  Remediation: Reverted the faulty selection algorithm; added additional unit + integration tests; deployment gating adjusted.
  Action items: list with owners and due dates.

Contacts and ownership (quick directory)
- Incident Commander rotation: sashas@redwood.ai (primary), aisha@redwood.ai (backup)
- Runtime oncall: #runtime-oncall (Slack)
- Infra oncall: infra-oncall@redwood.ai
- CS escalation: cs-leads@redwood.ai

Document history and governance
This page replaces ad-hoc checklists and consolidates communication kits and scenario templates. Owners must keep the page up-to-date and include any new templates derived from customer-facing incidents.

If you find missing scenarios or need an additional runbook added to the library, open a PR on the docs repo and ping @aisha for review.

    "id": "dsid_11b4dc5c498c472b9827a245f5a0720e",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/company-handbook/05_internal-tools/equitable-onboarding-and-role-access-playbook-2028.json",
    "title": "Equitable Onboarding and Role Access Playbook",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Equitable Onboarding and Role Access Playbook\",\n  \"space\": \"company-handbook\",\n  \"author\": \"Asha Patel\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"people-ops\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2028-02-15\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2028-07-01\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Diego Ramos\",\n    \"Maya Chen\",\n    \"Liam O'Connor\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"onboarding\",\n    \"access-control\",\n    \"roles\",\n    \"benefits\",\n    \"inclusive-hiring\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"body\": \"Overview:\\\\n\\\\nThis playbook defines a standardized, equity-focused process for onboarding new hires and contractors, assigning role ladders, and granting access to internal tools and benefits at Redwood. It consolidates checklists, role-to-access mappings, escalation paths, and temporary-access policies so teams can deliver consistent experiences while minimizing security risk and administrative overhead.\\\\n\\\\nPrinciples:\\\\n- Fast and predictable: new team members should have core access within 24 hours of start for standard hires and 72 hours for contractors requiring background checks.\\\\n- Least privilege by default: grant the minimum access necessary for the role, with clear escalation paths for additional privileges.\\\\n- Equity-first: ensure accommodations and benefit enrollments are automatic where possible and that managers are notified of outstanding tasks.\\\\n- Auditability: every access grant and exception must have an owner, a justification, and an expiration.\\\\n\\\\nScope:\\\\n- Applies to all full-time employees (FTE), part-time employees (PTE), and long-term contractors (>30 days).\\\\n- Excludes short contractors (<30 days) who receive a reduced, timeboxed access profile (see section \\\\\\\"Temporary contractor access\\\\\\\").\\\\n- Covers system access, hardware provisioning, benefits enrollment, and role ladder placement.\\\\n\\\\nRole Ladder & Access Matrix (excerpt):\\\\n| Role level | Typical title examples | Default access group(s) | Manager approval required? | People-ops review window |\\\\n|---|---|---:|:---:|---:|\\\\n| L1 - Associate | Associate SWE, Associate PM | core-read, email, slack | No | 24 hours |\\\\n| L2 - IC | SWE II, PM II | core-read, core-write, repo-ci | No | 24 hours |\\\\n| L3 - Senior IC | Senior SWE, Senior PM | core-read, core-write, prod-view | Yes (manager) | 48 hours |\\\\n| L4 - Staff / Lead | Staff SWE, Lead PM | prod-write, infra-console | Yes (manager + infra-owner) | 72 hours |\\\\n| L5 - Senior Staff / Dir | Dir Eng, Principal | infra-admin (request only), payroll-admin view | Yes (people-ops + security) | 5 business days |\\\\n\\\\nNotes: \\\\\\\"core-*\\\\\\\" groups include email, Slack, RedwoodPortal (SSO) and documentation access. \\\\\\\"prod-*\\\\\\\" groups require signed infra policies and manager justification.\\\\n\\\\nOnboarding Checklist (first 72 hours):\\\\n1. Pre-Start (people-ops): create HR profile, invite to RedwoodPortal, prepare equipment order, and schedule orientation.\\\\n2. Day 0 (IT/People-ops): provision laptop, default Slack/email access, enroll in SSO (RDW-SSO), and assign mentor.\\\\n3. Day 1 (Hiring Manager): complete role orientation, confirm role ladder level and responsibilities, and submit any additional access requests via RedwoodAccess.\\\\n4. Day 3 (Manager & Team): complete security training, assign initial project repo permissions, and verify access to CI/CD dashboards.\\\\n5. Day 30/60/90: checkpoint meetings, performance expectations, and benefits enrollment confirmation.\\\\n\\\\nAccess Request Workflows:\\\\n- Self-Serve (recommended):\\\\n  1. Use RedwoodPortal > Access Requests > Select role profile (L1-L5) or custom entitlement.\\\\n  2. Attach manager approval (email or single-click approval token).\\\\n  3. People-ops automatically verifies benefits enrollment and triggers provisioning pipelines.\\\\n- Manual (for exceptions):\\\\n  1. Manager files a ticket in ServiceDesk (tag: access-exception).\\\\n  2. Security reviews justification within 24 business hours.\\\\n  3. If approved, request includes an expiration date (default 30 days) and an assigned owner.\\\\n\\\\nCLI Example (for infra owners):\\\\n```\\\\n# Grant temporary read-only access to infra-console for user\\\\nrdwctl iam grant --user alice@redwood.ai --group infra-console-read --expires 2028-08-01 --reason \\\\\\\"oncall support\\\\\\\"\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nTool Access Mapping (default profiles):\\\\n| Tool | Purpose | Default profile | Request path |\\\\n|---|---|---|---|\\\\n| Slack | Team communication | core-read | auto via SSO onboarding |\\\\n| RedwoodRepo | Code hosting | repo-ci for L2+, repo-write for L3+ | RedwoodPortal (manager attach) |\\\\n| Infra Console | Production dashboards & controls | prod-view for L3, prod-write for L4 | Manager + infra-owner approval |\\\\n| Payroll & Benefits Portal | Compensation & benefits | hr-view for people-ops, payroll-init for managers | People-ops provisioning |\\\\n| CI/CD (Forge) | Build/Deploy pipelines | repo-ci | Auto if repo access granted |\\\\n\\\\nBenefits Activation Steps (within 30 days):\\\\n- Health & dental: People-ops auto-enrolls based on hire type; new hires must complete beneficiary forms in BenefitsPortal.\\\\n- Equity / RSUs: Grant letters are uploaded to CompensationHub and employees confirm tax residency via the payroll portal.\\\\n- Parental & sabbatical leave: Submit intent form in LeaveTracker; pre-approved for eligible employees and require manager + people-ops signoff.\\\\n- Hybrid/office stipend: One-time request through ExpensePortal; receipts accepted in 90 days.\\\\n\\\\nFirst 90 Days: Manager Playbook (high-level):\\\\n- Week 1: Role clarity, project onboarding, buddy pairing, and mandatory security refresher.\\\\n- End of Month 1: Deliverables check-in, early feedback, and benefits confirmation.\\\\n- End of Month 3: Formal 90-day review, career ladder calibration, and if applicable start of compensation review window.\\\\n\\\\nTemporary Contractor Access: \\\\n- Contractors receive a \\\\\\\"contractor-min\\\\\\\" profile by default (email, documentation read, limited repo access).\\\\n- Requests for elevated access must be approved by manager and people-ops and are timeboxed with automated revocation.\\\\n- Background checks required for access to production systems; provisioning blocked until check passes.\\\\n\\\\nExceptions & Audit Requirements:\\\\n- Any deviation from the role-to-access matrix must include: approver (manager name), justification, and expiration date.\\\\n- All exceptions are surfaced weekly to Security and People-Ops for review; long-running exceptions (>90 days) require executive sponsor.\\\\n\\\\nOwnership & SLAs:\\\\n- People-ops: owner for onboarding flow and benefits activation (SLA: 24 hours for core access provisioning).\\\\n- IT/Infrastructure: owner for hardware and privileged infra roles (SLA: 72 hours for hardware).\\\\n- Security: owner for exception review and sensitive access audits (SLA: 24 business hours for exception triage).\\\\n\\\\nCommon Scenarios & Quick Steps:\\\\n- Lost laptop: contact IT via ServiceDesk -> ticket auto-creates a device-revoke flow -> security locks account.\\\\n- Manager change of level (promotion): manager files \\\\\\\"role-change\\\\\\\" in RedwoodPortal -> people-ops updates HR profile -> infra provisioning updates group memberships.\\\\n\\\\nRelated pages:\\\\n- company-handbook/05_internal-tools/onboarding-toolchain-access-and-career-checkpoints-2025.json\\\\n- company-handbook/01_working-at-redwood/employee-success-pathways-and-tooling-handbook-2027.json\\\\n\\\\nAppendix: Standard templates (copyable)\\\\n- Manager approval justification (short):\\\\n  - Employee: {{name}} | Role: {{role}} | Justification: {{reason}} | Duration: {{days}} | Approver: {{manager}}\\\\n\\\\n- Exception record CSV header sample:\\\\n  employee_email,approver,justification,approved_on,expires_on,owner\\\\n\\\\nContact & Escalation:\\\\n- People-Ops ticket queue: people-ops@redwood.ai (monitored 08:00\\u201318:00 PT)\\\\n- On-call security pager: +1-555-0102 (for production access incidents)\\\\n- IT hardware team: it-ops@redwood.ai\\\\n\\\\nThis playbook is maintained by People Operations. Suggested updates should be submitted via the internal doc review workflow (RedwoodPortal -> Docs -> Edit Suggestion).\\\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_11b4dc5c498c472b9827a245f5a0720e\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Equitable Onboarding and Role Access Playbook\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/company-handbook/05_internal-tools/equitable-onboarding-and-role-access-playbook-2028.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: company-handbook\n\nbody : overview : \\ n \\ nthis playbook defines a standardized, equity - focused process for onboarding new hires and contractors, assigning role ladders, and granting access to internal tools and benefits at redwood. it consolidates checklists, role - to - access mappings, escalation paths, and temporary - access policies so teams can deliver consistent experiences while minimizing security risk and administrative overhead. \\ n \\ nprinciples : \\ n - fast and predictable : new team members should have core access within 24 hours of start for standard hires and 72 hours for contractors requiring background checks. \\ n - least privilege by default : grant the minimum access necessary for the role, with clear escalation paths for additional privileges. \\ n - equity - first : ensure accommodations and benefit enrollments are automatic where possible and that",

document.title: Equitable Onboarding and Role Access Playbook
document.content:
{
  "title": "Equitable Onboarding and Role Access Playbook",
  "space": "company-handbook",
  "author": "Asha Patel",
  "owner_team": "people-ops",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2028-02-15",
  "last_updated": "2028-07-01",
  "reviewers": [
    "Diego Ramos",
    "Maya Chen",
    "Liam O'Connor"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "onboarding",
    "access-control",
    "roles",
    "benefits",
    "inclusive-hiring"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "body": "Overview:\\n\\nThis playbook defines a standardized, equity-focused process for onboarding new hires and contractors, assigning role ladders, and granting access to internal tools and benefits at Redwood. It consolidates checklists, role-to-access mappings, escalation paths, and temporary-access policies so teams can deliver consistent experiences while minimizing security risk and administrative overhead.\\n\\nPrinciples:\\n- Fast and predictable: new team members should have core access within 24 hours of start for standard hires and 72 hours for contractors requiring background checks.\\n- Least privilege by default: grant the minimum access necessary for the role, with clear escalation paths for additional privileges.\\n- Equity-first: ensure accommodations and benefit enrollments are automatic where possible and that managers are notified of outstanding tasks.\\n- Auditability: every access grant and exception must have an owner, a justification, and an expiration.\\n\\nScope:\\n- Applies to all full-time employees (FTE), part-time employees (PTE), and long-term contractors (>30 days).\\n- Excludes short contractors (<30 days) who receive a reduced, timeboxed access profile (see section \\\"Temporary contractor access\\\").\\n- Covers system access, hardware provisioning, benefits enrollment, and role ladder placement.\\n\\nRole Ladder & Access Matrix (excerpt):\\n| Role level | Typical title examples | Default access group(s) | Manager approval required? | People-ops review window |\\n|---|---|---:|:---:|---:|\\n| L1 - Associate | Associate SWE, Associate PM | core-read, email, slack | No | 24 hours |\\n| L2 - IC | SWE II, PM II | core-read, core-write, repo-ci | No | 24 hours |\\n| L3 - Senior IC | Senior SWE, Senior PM | core-read, core-write, prod-view | Yes (manager) | 48 hours |\\n| L4 - Staff / Lead | Staff SWE, Lead PM | prod-write, infra-console | Yes (manager + infra-owner) | 72 hours |\\n| L5 - Senior Staff / Dir | Dir Eng, Principal | infra-admin (request only), payroll-admin view | Yes (people-ops + security) | 5 business days |\\n\\nNotes: \\\"core-*\\\" groups include email, Slack, RedwoodPortal (SSO) and documentation access. \\\"prod-*\\\" groups require signed infra policies and manager justification.\\n\\nOnboarding Checklist (first 72 hours):\\n1. Pre-Start (people-ops): create HR profile, invite to RedwoodPortal, prepare equipment order, and schedule orientation.\\n2. Day 0 (IT/People-ops): provision laptop, default Slack/email access, enroll in SSO (RDW-SSO), and assign mentor.\\n3. Day 1 (Hiring Manager): complete role orientation, confirm role ladder level and responsibilities, and submit any additional access requests via RedwoodAccess.\\n4. Day 3 (Manager & Team): complete security training, assign initial project repo permissions, and verify access to CI/CD dashboards.\\n5. Day 30/60/90: checkpoint meetings, performance expectations, and benefits enrollment confirmation.\\n\\nAccess Request Workflows:\\n- Self-Serve (recommended):\\n  1. Use RedwoodPortal > Access Requests > Select role profile (L1-L5) or custom entitlement.\\n  2. Attach manager approval (email or single-click approval token).\\n  3. People-ops automatically verifies benefits enrollment and triggers provisioning pipelines.\\n- Manual (for exceptions):\\n  1. Manager files a ticket in ServiceDesk (tag: access-exception).\\n  2. Security reviews justification within 24 business hours.\\n  3. If approved, request includes an expiration date (default 30 days) and an assigned owner.\\n\\nCLI Example (for infra owners):\\n```\\n# Grant temporary read-only access to infra-console for user\\nrdwctl iam grant --user alice@redwood.ai --group infra-console-read --expires 2028-08-01 --reason \\\"oncall support\\\"\\n```\\n\\nTool Access Mapping (default profiles):\\n| Tool | Purpose | Default profile | Request path |\\n|---|---|---|---|\\n| Slack | Team communication | core-read | auto via SSO onboarding |\\n| RedwoodRepo | Code hosting | repo-ci for L2+, repo-write for L3+ | RedwoodPortal (manager attach) |\\n| Infra Console | Production dashboards & controls | prod-view for L3, prod-write for L4 | Manager + infra-owner approval |\\n| Payroll & Benefits Portal | Compensation & benefits | hr-view for people-ops, payroll-init for managers | People-ops provisioning |\\n| CI/CD (Forge) | Build/Deploy pipelines | repo-ci | Auto if repo access granted |\\n\\nBenefits Activation Steps (within 30 days):\\n- Health & dental: People-ops auto-enrolls based on hire type; new hires must complete beneficiary forms in BenefitsPortal.\\n- Equity / RSUs: Grant letters are uploaded to CompensationHub and employees confirm tax residency via the payroll portal.\\n- Parental & sabbatical leave: Submit intent form in LeaveTracker; pre-approved for eligible employees and require manager + people-ops signoff.\\n- Hybrid/office stipend: One-time request through ExpensePortal; receipts accepted in 90 days.\\n\\nFirst 90 Days: Manager Playbook (high-level):\\n- Week 1: Role clarity, project onboarding, buddy pairing, and mandatory security refresher.\\n- End of Month 1: Deliverables check-in, early feedback, and benefits confirmation.\\n- End of Month 3: Formal 90-day review, career ladder calibration, and if applicable start of compensation review window.\\n\\nTemporary Contractor Access: \\n- Contractors receive a \\\"contractor-min\\\" profile by default (email, documentation read, limited repo access).\\n- Requests for elevated access must be approved by manager and people-ops and are timeboxed with automated revocation.\\n- Background checks required for access to production systems; provisioning blocked until check passes.\\n\\nExceptions & Audit Requirements:\\n- Any deviation from the role-to-access matrix must include: approver (manager name), justification, and expiration date.\\n- All exceptions are surfaced weekly to Security and People-Ops for review; long-running exceptions (>90 days) require executive sponsor.\\n\\nOwnership & SLAs:\\n- People-ops: owner for onboarding flow and benefits activation (SLA: 24 hours for core access provisioning).\\n- IT/Infrastructure: owner for hardware and privileged infra roles (SLA: 72 hours for hardware).\\n- Security: owner for exception review and sensitive access audits (SLA: 24 business hours for exception triage).\\n\\nCommon Scenarios & Quick Steps:\\n- Lost laptop: contact IT via ServiceDesk -> ticket auto-creates a device-revoke flow -> security locks account.\\n- Manager change of level (promotion): manager files \\\"role-change\\\" in RedwoodPortal -> people-ops updates HR profile -> infra provisioning updates group memberships.\\n\\nRelated pages:\\n- company-handbook/05_internal-tools/onboarding-toolchain-access-and-career-checkpoints-2025.json\\n- company-handbook/01_working-at-redwood/employee-success-pathways-and-tooling-handbook-2027.json\\n\\nAppendix: Standard templates (copyable)\\n- Manager approval justification (short):\\n  - Employee: {{name}} | Role: {{role}} | Justification: {{reason}} | Duration: {{days}} | Approver: {{manager}}\\n\\n- Exception record CSV header sample:\\n  employee_email,approver,justification,approved_on,expires_on,owner\\n\\nContact & Escalation:\\n- People-Ops ticket queue: people-ops@redwood.ai (monitored 08:00\u201318:00 PT)\\n- On-call security pager: +1-555-0102 (for production access incidents)\\n- IT hardware team: it-ops@redwood.ai\\n\\nThis playbook is maintained by People Operations. Suggested updates should be submitted via the internal doc review workflow (RedwoodPortal -> Docs -> Edit Suggestion).\\n",
  "title_field_name": "title",
  "content_field_names": [
    "body"
  ],
  "dataset_doc_uuid": "dsid_11b4dc5c498c472b9827a245f5a0720e"
}

    "id": "dsid_2ea2131de00f4d67878323beb975861b",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/known-issues/dispatcher-memory-leak-connection-windowing-2026.json",
    "title": "Dispatcher memory leak and connection-window exhaustion — investigation & mitigation",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Dispatcher memory leak and connection-window exhaustion \\u2014 investigation & mitigation\",\n  \"space\": \"eng-serving-runtime\",\n  \"author\": \"Maya Singh\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-02-12\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-07-03\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Ethan Brooks\",\n    \"Leah Martinez\",\n    \"Noah Adler\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"incident-response\",\n    \"memory-leak\",\n    \"dispatcher\",\n    \"connectivity\",\n    \"runbook\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"body\": \"Summary\\n-------\\nThis page documents a recurring failure class observed in the dispatcher service where long-running connection windows and an unbounded buffer growth lead to pod memory exhaustion and partial request loss. The doc covers: detection signals, short-term mitigations, permanent fixes planned, rollout steps, post-incident verification, and ownership.\\n\\nContext and scope\\n------------------\\n- Affected service: dispatcher-service (grpc frontend + connection multiplexer)\\n- Secondary impact: kernel-manager and grpc-proxy pods observed elevated tail latency due to request drops and retries.\\n- Customer-visible symptoms: increased 5xx rates on hosted API routes, transient model swap failures, and elevated p99 latency.\\n- Root hypothesis summary: under sustained backpressure (long KV cache fetches / slow kernel warmstarts), the dispatcher accumulates connection windows and request buffers that are not compacted, causing memory pressure and eventual OOM/kube eviction.\\n\\nWhy this matters\\n------------------\\n- SLO impact: incidents breached the 99.9% availability SLO for several customer routes for 4\\u201317 minutes in observed incidents.\\n- Cost/operational: repeated restarts mask the underlying problem and create downstream load spikes (thundering herd) when services recover.\\n\\nDetection and alerting\\n----------------------\\nCreate or verify these signals in Grafana / Prometheus: \\n1) Memory growth slope alert (dispatcher pod level):\\n- PromQL (example):\\n  increase(container_memory_working_set_bytes{job=\\\"dispatcher-service\\\"}[15m]) > 150e6\\n- Alert intent: signal sustained memory growth > 150MB over 15 minutes.\\n\\n2) Connection-window count spike:\\n- Instrumentation metric: dispatcher_connection_windows_total (gauge of active per-client windows)\\n- PromQL: sum(dispatcher_connection_windows_total) by(cluster_zone) > 5000\\n\\n3) Request buffer backlog:\\n- Metric: dispatcher_request_buffer_depth (histogram buckets or gauge). Alert when avg > 400 per pod for 10m.\\n\\n4) Error surface correlation: correlate 500s spike with buffer metrics using dashboards. Create a combined panel that shows: 5xx_rate, dispatcher_memory_working_set, request_buffer_depth\\n\\nInvestigation checklist (fast triage)\\n------------------------------------\\n1) Identify affected pods: kubectl -n inference get pods -l app=dispatcher-service --field-selector status.phase!=Running\\n2) Check last OOM reason: kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -i oom\\n3) Check top memory consumers inside the pod: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- pmap /proc/1/maps || ps aux --sort=-rss | head -n 20\\n4) Query metrics: use the PromQL alerts above to identify trend and onset time windows.\\n5) Grab heap profile (if enabled): curl -sS http://<pod-ip>:6060/debug/pprof/heap > heap-<pod>.pb.gz\\n6) Correlate with kernel-manager traces: tracer id / request ids in logs. Use the trace-id header to find full request timeline.\\n\\nImmediate mitigations (stop-gap, low-risk)\\n------------------------------------------\\nApply these in order to reduce customer-visible impact while preserving diagnostics: \\n1) Scale horizontally: kubectl scale --replicas=+2 deploy/dispatcher-service (add pods to lower per-pod backlog).\\n2) Enable admission backpressure: set config dispatcher.max_inflight_per_client to 50 (from default 200) via config map and rolling restart. This limits per-client window growth.\\n3) TTL/Compaction: reduce dispatcher.window_idle_ttl from 10m to 90s to force faster window tear-down.\\n4) Controlled rolling restart: restart the pods with highest memory slope first, one at a time, with 3m drain between restarts. Use the readiness probe to ensure no traffic is sent to the pod during restart.\\n5) Route heavy customers to Dedicated capacity or lower-priority model variants temporarily (use routing policy to steer by customer tag).\\n\\nPermanent remediation plan (engineering work items)\\n--------------------------------------------------\\nPriority and owner: platform/runtime team (owner: Maya Singh)\\nPlanned tasks and rationale: \\n- Task A (P0): Fix buffer compaction logic \\u2014 when downstream kernels take long to accept data, dispatcher should compact or spill oldest requests to disk-backed buffer with explicit backpressure. (PR: #5482)\\n- Task B (P1): Add bounded request queue per-client with adaptive eviction policies (evict smallest/least-progressing items).\\n- Task C (P1): Improve heap visibility \\u2014 enable continuous heap sampling and add an automated heap-diff alert with sample retention for 72 hours.\\n- Task D (P2): Add a new telemetry label to trace all requests carrying dispatcher_window_id for easier cross-service correlation.\\n- Task E (P2): Scheduler change \\u2014 enforce admission controls earlier in edge proxies to stop untrusted clients from opening many logical windows.\\nEstimated timeline: P0 in 3 weeks (hotfix + canary), P1/P2 in 6\\u201310 weeks with review cycles and integration tests.\\n\\nPatch / hotfix notes\\n--------------------\\n- Hotfix branches: hotfix/dispatcher/buffer-compact-2026-06 (contains limited compaction and conservative defaults).\\n- Canary plan: deploy to canary zone (us-west-canary) with 5% traffic shadowing for 48 hours and run the playback suite from benchmarking repo (endpoint: /health-playback).\\n- PR references: #5482 (compaction), #5510 (window-id telemetry).\\n\\nRollout checklist (post-PR merge)\\n--------------------------------\\n1) Deploy hotfix to staging and run the synthetic backlog test from benchmarking suite: benchmarks/runtime/dispatcher-backlog-sim (expected max memory < 1.2x baseline).\\n2) Canary deploy to us-west-canary with traffic-split=5% and monitor alerts for 24\\u201348 hours.\\n3) If no regressions, lift to 25% traffic for another 24 hours.\\n4) Gradually roll to remaining regions with guardrails: watch for memory-slope alert, request_buffer_depth, and 5xx_rate.\\n5) Complete rollout and mark release in release-tracker: release-id: rdr-runtime-2026-06-compact.\\n\\nRollback plan\\n-------------\\n- If memory slope increases by > 50% vs baseline or 5xx rate increases > 1% absolute during canary: rollback to previous deploy using kubectl rollout undo deployment/dispatcher-service --to-revision=<rev> and revert config changes (max_inflight_per_client, window_idle_ttl).\\n- For severe regressions, scale down the hotfix replicas and revert config through the operator to restore previous behavior.\\n\\nPost-incident verification and monitoring additions\\n--------------------------------------------------\\n- Add a derived metric: dispatcher_active_window_memory_ratio = dispatcher_memory_used_by_windows / container_memory_working_set_bytes. Alert if > 0.6 for 10m.\\n- Add an automated dashboard row in the dispatcher incident dashboard: memory slope, buffer depth, active windows, 5xx rate, kernel-manager inflight.\\n- Add unit and integration tests in the runtime bench suite that simulate slow kernel acceptance and verify compaction does not exceed memory targets.\\n\\nOwnership and escalation\\n------------------------\\n- Primary owner: Runtime Platform (oncall rotation: runtime-platform-oncall).\\n- Secondary owner: Serving Runtime SRE.\\n- Pager escalation: runtime-platform-oncall -> platform-lead -> eng-sre-lead.\\n- Slack channels: #runtime-ops, #serving-incident-escalations\\n\\nPostmortem and follow-ups\\n-------------------------\\n1) Run a two-week incident review with stakeholders: runtime, SRE, kernel-team, customer-success for any impacted customers.\\n2) Deliver a short RCA doc that enumerates timeline, root causes, and action items with target dates.\\n3) Close or convert any temporary mitigations (shorter TTLs, stricter admission) into configuration toggles that default to safe values.\\n\\nAppendices\\n---------\\nA) Example PromQL snippets\\n- Memory slope (per pod): increase(container_memory_working_set_bytes{pod=~\\\"dispatcher-service-.*\\\"}[10m])\\n- Buffer depth agg: avg_over_time(dispatcher_request_buffer_depth[5m])\\n- Combined alert rule sample:\\n  - name: DispatcherMemorySlope\\n    expr: increase(container_memory_working_set_bytes{job=\\\"dispatcher-service\\\"}[15m]) > 150e6\\n    for: 10m\\n\\nB) Diagnostic commands\\n1) pod list and memory usage: kubectl top pod -n inference | grep dispatcher-service\\\\2) fetch heap profile: kubectl exec -n inference -c dispatcher <pod> -- curl -sS localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap > /tmp/heap.pb.gz\\\\3) extract top alloc sites from heap: go tool pprof -top /tmp/heap.pb.gz\\\\\\\\n\\nC) Impact table (sample from incident 2026-06-18)\\n| Region | Duration | Peak affected pods | Customer routes impacted | Notes |\\n| us-west-2 | 00:17 | 3 | /v1/generate, /v1/chat | sustained KV fetch failure from remote cache |\\n| eu-central-1 | 00:04 | 1 | /v1/embed | transient kernel warmstart stutter |\\n\\nRelated pages\\n-------------\\n- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026 (for fallback policies)\\n- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/gpu-memory-fragmentation-diagnostics-playbook-2026 (for GPU memory correlation)\\n- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026 (benchmarks to run)\\n\\nContact and next steps\\n----------------------\\nIf you are paged, follow the Investigation checklist, apply Immediate mitigations as needed, and notify runtime-platform-oncall. For changes to telemetry or alerting, open an RFC in the runtime-team repo and tag reviewers: @EthanB, @LeahM.\\n\\nDocument history\\n----------------\\n- 2026-02-12: created by Maya Singh\\n- 2026-06-19: hotfix branch created and canary started (notes added)\\n- 2026-07-03: permanent remediation plan and rollout checklist added\\n\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_2ea2131de00f4d67878323beb975861b\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Dispatcher memory leak and connection-window exhaustion — investigation & mitigation\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/known-issues/dispatcher-memory-leak-connection-windowing-2026.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: eng-serving-runtime\n\nshort - term mitigations, permanent fixes planned, rollout steps, post - incident verification, and ownership. context and scope - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - affected service : dispatcher - service ( grpc frontend + connection multiplexer ) - secondary impact : kernel - manager and grpc - proxy pods observed elevated tail latency due to request drops and retries. - customer - visible symptoms : increased 5xx rates on hosted api routes, transient model swap failures, and elevated p99 latency. - root hypothesis summary : under sustained backpressure ( long kv cache fetches / slow kernel warmstarts ), the dispatcher accumulates connection windows and request buffers that are not compacted, causing memory pressure",
